clue.text: Recollection of news about old soldier

indicators.note: about says one piece goes round the other, here the scrambled news around the old letter
re-collection, gathering the letters together again, so the word for news is rearranged

parts.note: a report is a piece of news

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a news story about an old soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recollection of' is read as re-collection: REPORT rearranged gives TROPER, and 'about' puts it round O.
explanation.definitionFit: A trooper is a private soldier, especially in a cavalry or armoured regiment.

clue.text: Red male, little bit lacking in tail

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

indicators.note: lacking in tail says the last letter of the word is removed

parts.note: an atom is a tiny bit of something

explanation.surface: A red-faced man is missing a small piece of his tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomatoes are proverbially red; the fruit's name can stand as an example of something red.

clue.text: Having bandaged bad cut, sign people operating well?

indicators.note: having bandaged says the sign wraps round the next piece like a dressing

parts.note: an omen is a sign of things to come

indicators.note: cut says the word loses its last letter

parts.note: ill means bad

explanation.surface: Someone bandages a nasty cut and signs off fit to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well' is not about health: these people work an oil well.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil workers operate wells, here an oil well rather than good health.

clue.text: Ignored port that's old-fashioned?

parts.note: passé means out of date, old-fashioned
Dover is the English Channel port

explanation.surface: Someone declined the port, which seemed an old-fashioned after-dinner drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' suggests the drink passed round the table; it is the English Channel port.
explanation.definitionFit: To be passed over is to be overlooked, ignored in favour of someone else.

clue.text: Look up, one way or the other

definitions.note: to look something up in a reference is to consult it, the sense here

indicators.note: one way or the other says the word reads the same in both directions

parts.note: to look something up in a reference is to consult it, the sense here

explanation.surface: Consult a reference, whichever way you go.
explanation.definitionFit: To consult a reference book is to look something up in it.

clue.text: Something burning, opening blast rents asunder

indicators.note: rents asunder says one word tears the other apart and sits in the split

parts.note: a gap is an opening
to blast someone is to slam them, criticise them hard

explanation.surface: An explosion at an opening tears something that was burning apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rents asunder' is the container signal: the blast splits the opening and sits in the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A gas lamp is a light fuelled by burning gas, so it is literally something burning.

clue.text: Bit of fish seen without tail, might a cat have followed him?

definitions.text: might a cat have followed him?

parts.note: a gill is part of a fish

indicators.note: without tail says the last letter of the word is removed

parts.note: espied means seen

explanation.surface: A fish's tail is missing, and a cat may have been on the trail.
explanation.walkthrough: Dizzy Gillespie was a bebop trumpeter; 'cat' is jazz slang for a jazz fan, not a feline after fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Jazz fans were called cats, and a bebop trumpet star is someone such hipsters would follow.

clue.text: Sweetener coating a cake or bar?

indicators.note: coating says the sweetener goes round the letter

parts.note: a sop is something given to pacify or bribe, a sweetener

explanation.surface: Sugar icing on a cake or a chocolate bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweetener' is not sugar but a bribe or concession, SOP.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilet soap comes as a cake or a bar, both words used for a block of it.

clue.text: Picnicker, by the sound of it?

definitions.text: Picnicker, by the sound of it?

parts.words: Picnicker, by the sound of it?
parts.note: split as pic-nicker, a nicker or stealer of pics, that is pictures

explanation.surface: A person out for an alfresco meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Hear 'picnicker' as 'pic' (picture) plus 'nicker', British slang for a thief.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who nicks pictures, stealing paintings, is a burglar specialising in artworks.

clue.text: Phosphorus, maybe a bit

parts.note: P is the chemical symbol for phosphorus
a is an example of an article, the indefinite one

explanation.surface: Phosphorus might be a small part of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A particle is a tiny piece, a minute bit of matter.

clue.text: See 16
Getting into part, I'm embracing challenge most profoundly — and so I should!

definitions.text: Getting into part, I'm embracing challenge most profoundly — and so I should!

indicators.note: getting into says the following group goes inside the word for part

parts.note: a factor is a part or component of something

indicators.note: embracing says the letters of I'm wrap round the next piece

parts.note: taken as its letters without the apostrophe

indicators.note: most profoundly means the deepest point of the word challenge, its very middle letter

explanation.surface: An actor boasts of taking on a part and embracing a challenge wholeheartedly, as befits the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most profoundly' takes the centre letter of 'challenge', L; 'embracing' and 'Getting into' nest it inside I'M and the part. The whole clue describes a screen performer.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting into a part and embracing a challenge deeply is exactly what a screen performer is expected to do.

clue.text: See 28
Asian couple is talked about

indicators.note: talked about signals that the word for couple is spoken and a same-sounding word is written

parts.note: to couple is to tie together

explanation.surface: An Asian pair is the subject of gossip.
explanation.definitionFit: A Thai person comes from Thailand in South-East Asia, so is an Asian.

clue.text: Old sport, through which one might join the action, did you say?

indicators.note: did you say asks us to hear the phrase spoken and write a same-sounding word

parts.words: through which one might join the action
parts.note: a doorway into a fight would be a battle door

explanation.surface: An old game is described as a way into the fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: Battledore and shuttlecock was the forerunner of badminton.
explanation.definitionFit: Battledore was an old game played with a small racket and a shuttlecock, ancestor of badminton.

clue.text: Energy invested in design of a logo, shape of a tube

indicators.note: invested in says energy's letter is placed inside the rearranged letters
a design of these words is a new pattern made from their letters

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Energy is put into designing a logo in the shape of a tube.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shape' looks like part of the definition but is anagram fodder: 'design of' rearranges A LOGO SHAPE into OESOPHAGAL, and 'invested in' adds E.
explanation.definitionFit: The oesophagus is the muscular tube from throat to stomach, and the adjective describes things belonging to it.

clue.text: Forward movement not entirely substandard, guru admits

indicators.note: admits says the guru lets the shortened word in

parts.note: a sage is a wise teacher, a guru

indicators.note: not entirely says the word loses its final letter

parts.note: crummy means shoddy, substandard

explanation.surface: A guru concedes that some progress is not quite up to standard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' means rugby forwards, who push together in a scrum; 'not entirely' drops the last letter and 'admits' puts the rest inside the guru.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby the forwards push against each other in a scrum, a movement made by the forwards.

clue.text: One leg in the air, donning knickers in public places

indicators.note: donning says the underwear is put on, wrapping round the hopping

parts.note: smalls is British slang for underwear such as knickers
hopping is moving with one leg raised off the ground

explanation.surface: Someone balances on one leg while pulling on their knickers in public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smalls' is British slang for underwear; 'donning' has the knickers go round the hopping.
explanation.definitionFit: Shopping malls are large public places where people gather to shop.

clue.text: Inspector of property (ours very unreliable)

indicators.note: unreliable suggests the letters cannot be trusted to stay in order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: The man checking our house is not to be trusted.
explanation.definitionFit: A building assessor examines property, checking its condition and value for buyers.

clue.text: Time required to tour Med, say, relax restriction on leaving home

indicators.note: to tour says the time goes round the sea

parts.note: an hour is a unit of time
the Mediterranean is an example of a sea
to rest is to relax

explanation.surface: A holiday tour of the Mediterranean followed by relaxation ends up as a ban on going out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to tour' puts the time round the sea; 'Med' is short for the Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: House arrest is detention in one's own home, a legal restriction forbidding the person from going out.

clue.text: Devil eggs in audition for restaurant?

indicators.note: in audition means heard rather than read, so a same-sounding word is written

parts.note: the beast is a name for the devil; roe is fish eggs

explanation.surface: A restaurant tries out devilled eggs on its menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Devil eggs' sounds like a recipe; spoken as 'beast roe' it sounds like a small café-restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: A bistro is a small, informal restaurant.

clue.text: Literary group gets stressed reading aloud?

indicators.note: reading aloud means the words are spoken and a same-sounding word is written

parts.note: someone stressed frays, as in frayed nerves

explanation.surface: A book club gets nervous when it has to read aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary group' suggests a book club; it is a group of words.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase is a small group of words in a piece of writing, a literary group.

clue.text: Pudding appearing very enticing initially, put on a stone or two?

definitions.text: put on a stone or two?

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of each of the four words before it

explanation.surface: An enticing pudding threatens to add a stone or two to the waistline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on a stone' suggests weight gain from the pudding; it really means laying paving stones.
explanation.definitionFit: To pave a surface is to lay flagstones on it, putting a stone or two in place.

clue.text: Ruin arch, crushing above

indicators.note: crushing says one word is squeezed inside the other

parts.note: arch in the sense of cheeky or mischievous means impish
over means above

explanation.surface: A collapsing arch crushes what lies above it, a ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arch' is not a structure but the adjective meaning mischievous; 'crushing' squeezes one word inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruin someone financially is to make them poor, to beggar them.

clue.text: Check in books for runner

indicators.note: in says the check sits inside the abbreviation for the books

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books
to vet is to check

explanation.surface: Checking library books for a runner.
explanation.walkthrough: Steve Ovett was a British middle-distance runner, Olympic 800m champion in 1980.
explanation.definitionFit: Steve Ovett was an Olympic gold medal athlete over 800 metres, a famous runner.

clue.text: Experienced woman taking £800?

indicators.note: taking means taking only the share named, four of the five letters, so the final one goes

parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand pounds; the question mark warns that only eight hundred of it, four-fifths, is wanted

explanation.surface: A seasoned woman takes home eight hundred pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: A grand is slang for £1000; £800 is four-fifths of it, so four of its five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandmother is an older woman, experienced in life.

clue.text: Aggressive, any fierce criminal

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters have gone wrong, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Any fierce criminal is an aggressive type.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase describes something confrontational and provocative, so aggressive in style.

clue.text: Seen from behind in portrait, some Roman port

indicators.note: Seen from behind says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone in a portrait is seen from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden word: the letters run across 'portrait, some' and are then read backwards, with 'in' signalling the hidden word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostia was the ancient harbour city at the mouth of the Tiber serving Rome.

clue.text: French department eroding and ignored, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone awry, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A French region suffers erosion and is neglected by the authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: A double anagram: 'eroding' and 'ignored' each rearrange to the answer, with 'unfortunately' as the signal for both.
explanation.definitionFit: Gironde is an administrative department in south-west France, around Bordeaux.

clue.text: Dog kennels re-home strays, those all welcome

indicators.note: kennels as a verb means houses, so the dog holds the other letters inside

parts.note: a terrier is a breed of dog

indicators.note: strays means the letters wander out of order

parts.note: them is a colloquial word for those

explanation.surface: A dog shelter rehomes strays, and everyone is welcome to come.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strays' looks like a noun but is the anagram signal, turning RE-HOME into HEMORE; 'kennels' as a verb means houses, putting that and the word for those inside the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says that a larger crowd makes for more fun, an invitation for everyone to join in.
